transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
House Republicans defeated an impeachment effort targeting Pete Hegseth, President Trump's
Secretary of Defense, the vote to effectively block the impeachment charges from being considered
passed 211 to 204, as NPR's Eric McDaniel reports.
Kentucky Republican Representative Thomas Massie spearheaded this impeachment effort
on his way out of Congress.
And the charges he filed were tied to failure to get congressional approval for military
action in Iran and Yemen, as well as strikes against what the administration says are drugboats
in the Caribbean and Pacific, and a Pentagon effort to publish a Democratic Senator, Mark
Kelly of Arizona, who told service members not to follow illegal orders.
Hegseth called the charges a sham, and the White House backed him up.
Most Republicans, even those openly critical of the administration's relationship with
Congress in terms of war powers, agree.
The impeachment effort is now dead.
Eric McDaniel, NPR News Capitol Hill.
The Republican-led House Oversight Committee says the Trump administration mishandled the
release of records related to Jeffrey Epstein in a new report.
The committee faults the administration for missing deadlines and failing to protect victims'
identities.
The report comes nearly a year after Congress required the release of the documents.
Democrats have used the issue to accuse Republicans of protecting the wealthy.
ExxonMobil is exploring a return to Venezuela after leaving almost two decades ago.
NPR's Julia Simon reports the U.S. oil giant is evaluating potential oil exploration and
production opportunities there.
ExxonMobil has had a rocky history in Venezuela.
It left the country in 2007.
In January, the Trump administration captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
And since then, the country has overhauled its petroleum law, making it more attractive
for international oil companies.
Chevron and Continental resources are increasing investments.
ExxonMobil is striking a more cautious tone.
An ExxonMobil spokesperson tells NPR that a newly signed memorandum of understanding
is a meaningful first step, but, quote, "any future investment would require stable policies,
clear regulations, strong investment protections, and competitive returns."
Julia Simon, NPR News.
Inflation in October was hotter than forecasters anticipated.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports on the latest cost of living index from the Labor Department.
Consumer prices in October were up four-tenths of a percent from September.
That's a smaller increase than the previous month, but inflation's still higher than
forecasters had expected.
Food prices increased sharply during the month, as did the cost of housing.
Stripping out volatile food and energy prices, core inflation was three-tenths of a percent,
also higher than forecasters had predicted.
The hot inflation reading underscores investors' expectation that the Federal Reserve will
raise its benchmark interest rate next month.
Markets were expecting a quarter-point increase, but Fed Governor Chris Waller suggested today
an even bigger rate hike might be appropriate to help bring prices under control.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
U.S. stocks fell today.
The S&P 500 lost nearly four-tenths of a percent.
This is NPR.
An appeals court says a federal judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge
journalists' communications to the Trump administration for a leak investigation.
The ruling says the government isn't entitled to a blanket order for LinkedIn to disclose
a broad array of user records belonging to the journalists.
The three-judge panel says journalists' First Amendment rights must be balanced against
the administration's duty to protect national security information.
Federal prosecutors have charged three more people in connection with a human smuggling
operation that left seven migrants, including a 14-year-old boy dead in South Texas earlier
this year, from Texas public radio Diego Medell reports.
In May, six migrants were found dead inside a shipping container at a Union Pacific rail
yard in Laredo.
A seventh was found dead near railroad tracks in San Antonio.
Prosecutors say smugglers discovered the migrants in distress when the train arrived from Del
Rio, abandoning one near the tracks in San Antonio and leaving the other six inside as
the train continued toward Laredo.
A grand jury indicted 11 people in July, but that number has now climbed to 14.
The expanded indictments include charges of money laundering and illegally bringing migrants
into the country.
Twelve defendants face up to life in prison if convicted.
For NPR News, I'm Diego Medell in San Antonio.
The family farm where President Jimmy Carter grew peanuts, corn, and sugarcane as a boy
in return throughout his life will be preserved and open to the public.
Preservation Group The Conservation Fund says the farm should be open to the public for
hunting, fishing, and recreation as soon as next year.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: House Republicans defeat impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, 211-204
House Oversight Committee report faults Trump administration over mishandled Jeffrey Epstein records release
ExxonMobil exploring return to Venezuela after leaving the country in 2007
October inflation runs hotter than forecasters expected, with food and housing costs rising
Appeals court narrows order requiring LinkedIn to disclose journalists' communications in leak probe
Three more people charged in South Texas human smuggling case that killed seven migrants
Jimmy Carter's boyhood family farm in Georgia to be preserved and opened to the public
